newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish debt office studies ways to lift liquidity.
newsitem.headline: Swedish debt office studies ways to lift liquidity.

text.p: Sweden's National Debt Office on Tuesday said it was considering ways to increase Treasury bill market liquidity as part of its efforts to improve the efficiency of the Swedish government securities market.

"One source of liquidity is always an efficient repo market and there may be ways in which the repo market for bills can be improved," said Thomas Franzen, head of the debt office, according to a printed copy of a speech to be given in London.
"Another possibility would be to limit the number of outstanding maturities in the bills market," he said.
Currently, the debt office has 12 maturities, with one bill maturing each month one year into the future.
"One could consider reducing this to four or five maturities, for example by having bills maturing in March, June, September and December in keeping with international market conventions," he said.
Regarding nominal bonds, issues may be concentrated to fewer maturities, Franzen said.
"In keeping with international practice, issues would primarily be in the two- to three-year, five- and 10-year segments and for longer than 10 years," he said.
Franzen also said he believed there will be futures trade in crown bonds.
"How and when futures trade in crown bonds may start are still open issues, but it is my belief that we will go in this direction, sooner or later," he said.
Looking at index linked bonds, Franzen said he expected the stock to continue expanding.

"Given the low borrowing needs, the rate of growth is likely to fall substantially compared to this year," he said. "But the debt office will be flexible in its issuance policy, adjusting it to the conditions in the market."
The debt office will continue to manage debt in such a way that the crown bond market remains attractive to investors, according to Franzen.
"High liquidity is essential, but there are also other elements in the market infrastructure that should be taken into account," Franzen concluded.
